title: Phishing in 90 seconds
subtitle: The rules, one hunt and two emails. Same app, faster.

cards.title: Protect yourself first
cards.say: I can't look after anyone if my own logins are wide open. Neither can you. So we start with you.

rules.headline: Read the domain after the @.
rules.body: Every letter. thisistea.example and thisistae-app.example belong to two different owners.

rules.headline: Notice the rush.
rules.body: A two-hour deadline is a feeling someone else put in you. Feelings aren't evidence.

rules.headline: Never type a password after clicking an email link.
rules.body: Open the site yourself, from a bookmark or by typing the address.

cards.sign_off: Zero trust isn't paranoia. It's checking.

cards.title: Shield the whole shell
cards.say: In all my years I've learned one thing: a single open door lets the tide into every room. When you guard your inbox, you guard your neighbours too. It works a little like a vaccine.

rules.headline: Confirm the unusual, together.
rules.body: A wire transfer, a password reset, an urgent file: check it on another channel. A phone call costs one minute.

rules.headline: Tell the others.
rules.body: If a strange email reached you, it reached your colleagues too. Report it to IT so we can warn everyone.

rules.headline: Give the whole team a second lock.
rules.body: With multi-factor authentication, one stolen password is a scratch, not a crack in the shell.

cards.sign_off: A team we can trust is a team that looks out for each other.

hunt.intro: I hid three tricks in that email. Click whatever you think is a trap. I won't say whether you're getting warm.

flags.title: The address
flags.spider_says: I swapped two letters and moved one word. Who reads every letter when they're worried?

flags.title: The clock
flags.spider_says: "Within 2 hours." Panic is my favourite accomplice. It quiets the part of you that checks.

flags.title: The ask
flags.spider_says: ThisIsTea would never ask for your password by email. But I sounded like ThisIsTea, and that was enough.

hunt.debrief: Every trick he just bragged about is one of my three rules. Address, rush, password. Go back and read them once more.

recovery.title_caught: If a real one ever gets you, dear, do this.
recovery.lead_caught: This time it was only practice and nothing was taken. A real one happens to the careful ones too, and then what matters is how fast we close the door. Here is the list.
recovery.title_default: Keep this plan in your pocket
recovery.lead_default: You walked past this one. Someday one will look better. Here is the five-step rescue plan: knowing it by heart is half the cure.

steps.headline: Change the password, on the real site.
steps.body: Open the site yourself, from a bookmark or by typing the address, never through the email. Then change that same password anywhere else you reused it.

steps.headline: Turn on multi-factor authentication.
steps.body: A second lock means a stolen password alone no longer opens the door.

steps.headline: Tell IT or security straight away.
steps.body: If you can, forward the email as an attachment. Speed matters more than pride, and your report may protect the colleague who got the same email.

steps.headline: Look for strange activity.
steps.body: Check the sign-in history and connected devices, and look for mail rules that forward or delete messages. Sign out anywhere you don't recognise.

steps.headline: Expect a second attempt.
steps.body: Attackers often follow up with a message that mentions the first one. Stay suspicious for the next few weeks.
